## 14.5 Tcl Compilers

There are some problems using Tcl in the commercial world. One is that you need to distribute the source code for your scripts. Another is that users must have the proper version of Tcl installed to run your script.

### 14.5 Tcl Compilers

The compilers generate Tcl bytecode files or complete executable programs. Shipping bytecode files will hide your source, and shipping an executable program allows the user to execute your application without having to install a Tcl interpreter and libraries.

### 14.5.1 ICEM Tcl Compiler

| Language | executable |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Site | http://icemcmfd.tcl/ice.html |
| Contact | tcl@icemcmfd.com |
| Tcl Revision | 7.4-8.0 Tk: 4.0-8.0 |
| Supported Platforms | DEC OS V4.0, HP-UX 9.0, IBM AIX 3.2, 4.1, Slackware 2.3 (ELF), SGI IRIX 5.x and above, Sparc Solaris 5.3 and up, Windows NT 4.0 and Win95 |

Interpreted code is fast to develop but runs slowly, whereas compiled code runs quickly but is slow to develop. The ICE Tcl compiler helps you get the best of both worlds. The compiler comes in two varieties. The version 1.3 compiler compiles Tcl 7.X scripts into C. This can speed up your script by factors between 5 and 15. The C output is compiled and linked with Tcl libraries to create an executable. The compiled C code produced by 1.3 compiler is about 50% faster than the interpreted Tcl 8.0 code. The version 2.0 compiler (under development until 1998) will be able to generate Tcl object code, Java code, or C object code and will perform optimizations including constant folding, subexpression elimination, and loop unrolling.

### 14.5.2 Plus-Patch

| Language | C |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Site | http://home.wxs.nl/~nijmans/ |
| Contact | Jan.nijmans@wxs.nl |
| Tcl Revision Supported | Tcl: 7.6-8.1 Tk: 4.2-8.1 |
| Supported Platforms | Unix, MS-Windows 95, MS-Windows NT |

The plus-patch lets you develop your script in Tcl/Tk and create an executable for distribution. This does this by creating a C language wrapper around the script so that you can compile the wrapper and link it with Tcl/Tk initialization files and libraries. The executable is not small, but many programs are small. Converting a script to an executable with this package is fast and easy.

The procedure to create a standalone application:

- 1. Download the plus-patch. You may download either the patches or the complete Tcl/Tk distribution with patches. The complete code is supplied as zip files and gzipped tar files.
- 2. If you downloaded the patch kit, apply it to your Tcl/Tk distribution. If you downloaded the complete code with patches, unpack the distribution.
- 3. Compile the patched code. Use the same procedure as for a standard Tcl distribution: Cd to the appropriate directory for your OS (win or unix).
- 4. Create and debug your Tcl/Tk application.
- 5. Run tcl2c to create a C wrapper around the Tcl script. The command line will resemble:
```
tcl2c -o myFile.c -tk myFile.tk
```
- 6. Compile and link the .c file with Tcl-plus libraries. Under Unix this can be done with a command such as:
```
cc myFile.c /usr/local/lib/libtk8.0.a \
/usr/local/lib/tcl8.0.a -L/usr/local/lib/X11 -lX11 -lsocket -lm
```

Under Windows you can modify the Makefile in the win directory (Makefile.vc for Microsoft C++ or Makefile.bc for Borland C++). The Makefile contains entries to convert the hello.tcl example script into hello.exe. If you change the entries for hello to the name of your program, you can make package using this Makefile.

If you are using VC++ 5.0, you can use the Visual C++ 5.0 development tools included with the tcl82plus.exe distribution. The hello.tcl script is supplied with the plus-patch kit to demonstrate how an executable can be built. The tcl2c program turns your Tcl script into a set of data definitions within a new C module. This module includes a main entry point that initializes the Tcl interpreter and then executes your script using a series of Tcl_Eval function calls to pass the script lines to the interpreter.

### 14.5.3 TclPro Compiler

| Language | executable |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Site | http://www.scripts.com |
| Contact | sales@scripts.com |
| Tcl Revision Supported | Tcl: 8.0.3 Tk: 8.0.3 |
| Supported Platforms | Unix, Windows NT, 95 |

The TclPro Compiler will turn a Tcl script into a set of Tcl bytecodes that can load and run on any platform. The bytecode files can be read with an extension that is part of the TclPro package. This extension may be distributed by developers but is not part of the standard Tcl 8.0.3 release. The bytecode files run faster than a pure script program (since there is no need for the just-in-time compilation) and are effective in concealing your program.

In the first beta release of TclPro Compiler the bytecode file may be slightly larger than the original script file. The bytecode file is generated as an ASCII representation of the binary bytecodes. The official release of the Tcl Compiler will produce smaller files.

## 14.6 Packaging Tools

One of the other problems with distributing Tcl packages and applications has been associated with installation. Some packages require that users modify a Makefile to define where the libraries and interpreter are stored on their system. Other packages have a startup-script that will either query the user or search in known places for libraries and interpreters.

Jan Nijmans's plus-patch provides one solution to that problem by linking a Tcl script with the libraries and interpreters to create a single file executable.

This technique has problems if your application requires several files, rather than a single script.

Tclutor uses the plus-patch and tcl2c to create an installation program that moves the TTutor program, lesson files, etc. into an installation directory. This works fairly well, but experience shows about 1 in 500 users misinstall the program.

### 14.6.1 Scripts TclPro Wrapper

| Language | executable |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Site | http://www.scripts.com |
| Contact | sales@scripts.com |
| Tcl Revision Supported | Tcl: 8.0.3 Tk: 8.0.3 |
| Supported Platforms | Unix, Windows NT, Windows 95 |

The Scripts TclPro Wrapper combines a set of Tcl script files, Tcl bytecode files, images, etc. into a single executable file that combines the functionality of an archive and an application. You can even include your own tcl (or wish) interpreter and libraries in this executable file.

You can declare one script file within the bundle of files combined by TclPro Wrapper to be evaluated by the Tcl interpreter. This file may be evaluated by the interpreter included in the bundle or by an interpreter already
